items.stem: Which colour of visible light has the highest energy per photon?
items.answer: violet
items.markingKey: violet. Violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Each line in the hydrogen spectrum is produced when an electron jumps up to a higher energy level." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Emission lines come from electrons falling from higher to lower levels and emitting photons; promotion absorbs energy (absorption spectrum).
items.markingKey: Emission lines come from electrons falling from higher to lower levels and emitting photons; promotion absorbs energy (absorption spectrum). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: As the frequency of electromagnetic radiation increases, which also increases?
items.answer: photon energy
items.markingKey: D. E = hf; c is constant so λ falls.

items.stem: Calculate the energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, carried by one mole of photons of wavelength 253.7 nm.
items.answer: 472 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem:

Electron removed | IE / kJ mol⁻¹ | log₁₀(IE)

(b) Identify the position of the largest increase and deduce the group number of the element. [2]
(c) Write an equation for the second ionisation energy of the element. [1]
(d) Explain why each successive ionisation energy is greater than the previous one. [2]
(e) Identify the element. [1]

items.answer: (a) The values cover a very wide range; a log scale allows all the values and the jumps to be seen clearly on one graph. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The Bohr model of the atom is adequate for explaining atomic spectra."
items.answer: Bohr explains hydrogen well but is limited; the orbital (quantum mechanical) model is needed for multi-electron atoms – theories are refined in light of evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains the hydrogen line spectrum and convergence quantitatively; introduces quantised energy levels. Arguments against: fails for atoms with more than one electron; cannot explain sublevels, orbital shapes or relative line intensities; replaced by quantum mechanical model with orbitals. Supported judgement: Bohr explains hydrogen well but is limited; the orbital (quantum mechanical) model is needed for multi-electron atoms – theories are refined in light of evidence.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "continuous spectrum"?
options: A representation of electron configuration in which each orbital is drawn as a box and electrons as arrows showing spin
A spectrum containing all wavelengths (colours) over a range, with no gaps, such as that of white light
The decrease in spacing between spectral lines at higher frequency, as energy levels get closer together
An arrangement in which one or more electrons occupy higher energy levels than in the ground state
items.answer: A spectrum containing all wavelengths (colours) over a range, with no gaps, such as that of white light
items.markingKey: B. "continuous spectrum" is a spectrum containing all wavelengths (colours) over a range, with no gaps, such as that of white light.

items.stem: Distinguish between an absorption spectrum and an emission spectrum.
items.answer: An emission spectrum shows bright lines from photons emitted as electrons fall to lower levels; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines at the same frequencies where photons are absorbed as electrons are promoted.
items.markingKey: An emission spectrum shows bright lines from photons emitted as electrons fall to lower levels; an absorption spectrum shows dark lines at the same frequencies where photons are absorbed as electrons are promoted. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the hydrogen emission spectrum consists of lines rather than a continuous band.
items.answer: Electrons can only occupy fixed (quantised) energy levels; each line corresponds to a transition between two levels and so a photon of one specific energy (frequency, E = hf).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Electrons can only occupy fixed (quantised) energy levels; each line corresponds to a transition between two levels and so a photon of one specific energy (frequency, E = hf). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
The frequencies of lines in the Lyman series of hydrogen were measured. The difference Δf between each line and the next was calculated.

f / 10¹⁵ Hz | Δf / 10¹⁵ Hz
2.468 | 0.456
2.924 | 0.160
3.084 | 0.074
3.158 | 0.041
3.199 | 0.024

(a) Explain why Δf decreases as f increases. [1]
(b) Describe how a graph of Δf against f can be used to find the convergence limit. [2]
(c) The convergence limit is found to be 3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Calculate the ionisation energy of hydrogen in kJ mol⁻¹. [2]
(d) State why the frequencies of lines close to the convergence limit have a larger uncertainty. [1]
(e) Explain why this series, rather than the visible series, must be used. [1]
(f) State why the measurements should be repeated at least three times. [1]
items.answer: (a) The energy levels get closer together at higher n, so successive lines are closer in energy/frequency. (b) Plot Δf (y) against f (x), draw a line of best fit and extrapolate to Δf = 0; the f-intercept is the convergence frequency. (c) 1310 kJ mol⁻¹ (d) The lines are very close together and difficult to resolve. (e) Only the series ending at n = 1 (the ground state) relates to removal of an electron from the ground state. (f) To identify anomalous results and to reduce the effect of random errors by calculating a mean.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] Levels converge at high n (1). (b) [2] Plot and best-fit curve/line (1); extrapolate to Δf = 0 (1). (c) [2] E = hf = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (M1); × NA/1000 = 1310 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1). (d) [1] Lines crowd together/hard to resolve (1). (e) [1] Ground state n = 1 (1). (f) [1] Identifies anomalies / reduces random error by averaging (1).

items.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from n = 7 to n = 2. Which describes the emitted radiation?
items.answer: ultraviolet, wavelength 398 nm
items.markingKey: A. ΔE = 1312(1/2² − 1/7²) kJ mol⁻¹ → λ = 398 nm (ultraviolet; transitions to n = 1 are UV, to n = 2 visible).

items.answer: Bohr explains hydrogen well but is limited; the orbital (quantum mechanical) model is needed for multi-electron atoms – theories are refined in light of evidence.

items.stem: Which sublevel is filled immediately after 4s?
items.answer: 3d
items.markingKey: B. Aufbau order: 4s then 3d then 4p.

items.stem: Which principle is violated by the ground-state configuration 1s² 2s¹ 2p¹ for beryllium?
items.answer: the Aufbau principle
items.markingKey: B. 2s is lower in energy and should be filled first (this is an excited state).

items.stem: A student claims: "The third energy level can hold only 8 electrons." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: n = 3 can hold 2n² = 18 electrons (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰); 8 is the number in 3s and 3p only.
items.markingKey: n = 3 can hold 2n² = 18 electrons (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰); 8 is the number in 3s and 3p only. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the full electron configuration of an atom with 9 electrons and identify the element.
items.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ (F)
items.markingKey: 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ – correct order and superscripts (A1); 1 mark deducted for any wrong sublevel occupancy. Element: F.

items.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of vanadium (Z = 23)?
items.answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³ 4s²
items.markingKey: C. V has 23 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³ 4s².

items.stem: An atom has the ground-state electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴. Which element is it?
items.answer: Se
items.markingKey: B. Total electrons = 34 → selenium.

items.stem: For an atom of phosphorus (Z = 15): (a) write the full electron configuration; (b) draw (describe) the orbital diagram for its highest-energy sublevel using arrows; (c) state the number of unpaired electrons and explain the reason in terms of Hund’s rule and the Pauli principle.
items.markingKey: (a) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³ (A1). (b) 3p orbitals [↑] [↑] [↑] – singly filled first, parallel spins (A1). (c) 3 unpaired (A1); degenerate orbitals singly occupied before pairing to minimise repulsion; paired electrons have opposite spins (Pauli) (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Aufbau principle correctly predicts the electron configuration of every element."
items.answer: Aufbau is a useful guideline but not a law; real configurations depend on subtle energy balances.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: correct for most of the first 36 elements; gives a systematic basis for the periodic table. Arguments against: exceptions such as Cr and Cu (and many heavier elements) exist; sublevel energies change with nuclear charge and electron number, e.g. 3d below 4s once filled; predicted order of ion formation (4s lost first) is not obvious from filling order. Supported judgement: Aufbau is a useful guideline but not a law; real configurations depend on subtle energy balances. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available first"?
items.answer: Aufbau principle
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Aufbau principle.

items.stem: Explain, using Hund's rule, why a nitrogen atom has three unpaired electrons.
items.answer: N is 1s² 2s² 2p³. The three 2p orbitals are degenerate; electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing because this minimises repulsion, so each 2p orbital holds one electron.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: N is 1s² 2s² 2p³. The three 2p orbitals are degenerate; electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing because this minimises repulsion, so each 2p orbital holds one electron. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between an s orbital and a p orbital.
items.answer: An s orbital is spherical and each s sublevel has one orbital; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped and each p sublevel has three orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles.
items.markingKey: An s orbital is spherical and each s sublevel has one orbital; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped and each p sublevel has three orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: State the total number of electrons in p orbitals in an atom of oxygen. (Z = 8)
items.markingKey: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴: p electrons = 4 (A1).

items.markingKey: 6. [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹: five 3d + one 4s.

items.stem: Explain why Fe³⁺ is more stable than Fe²⁺ with respect to further oxidation in many environments.
items.answer: Fe³⁺ has a half-filled [Ar] 3d⁵ configuration, with each d orbital singly occupied, which is relatively stable (lower repulsion); Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) has one paired d electron.

items.answer: K⁺

items.answer: [Ar] 3d⁷

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Exceptions such as chromium and copper show that the Aufbau principle is not useful."
items.answer: Aufbau remains a valuable rule of thumb; exceptions refine rather than invalidate it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real configurations deviate from predictions; heavier elements show even more exceptions. Arguments against: Aufbau correctly predicts almost all of the first 36 elements; exceptions can be explained by the small 3d/4s energy gap and the stability of half-filled/full sublevels. items.answer: A full configuration lists every occupied sublevel from 1s; a condensed configuration replaces the inner electrons with the symbol of the preceding noble gas in brackets.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "effective nuclear charge"?
options: The net positive charge experienced by an outer electron, equal to the nuclear charge reduced by shielding from inner electrons
An arrangement in which one or more electrons occupy higher energy levels than in the ground state
The pattern of specific frequencies (lines) of electromagnetic radiation emitted when excited electrons fall to lower energy levels
A spectrum consisting of discrete lines at particular frequencies, produced by transitions between fixed energy levels
items.answer: The net positive charge experienced by an outer electron, equal to the nuclear charge reduced by shielding from inner electrons
items.markingKey: A. "effective nuclear charge" is the net positive charge experienced by an outer electron, equal to the nuclear charge reduced by shielding from inner electrons.

items.stem: Which shows the general trend in first ionisation energy across a period and down a group?
items.answer: increases across, decreases down
items.markingKey: A. Effective nuclear charge vs distance/shielding.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the first ionisation energy generally increases across period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main energy level, so shielding stays roughly constant; the effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so outer electrons are held more strongly. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main energy level, so shielding stays roughly constant; the effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so outer electrons are held more strongly. items.stem: "Ionisation energy decreases across a period because the number of electrons increases." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: IE generally increases across a period: extra electrons go into the same energy level with little extra shielding while the nuclear charge increases.

items.stem: Explain the difference between first ionisation energy and second ionisation energy.
items.answer: First IE removes one electron from a gaseous atom (X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻); second IE removes an electron from the gaseous 1+ ion (X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻) and is always larger.

the visible series ending at n = 2

items.stem: The convergence limit of the ground-state series in the spectrum of a gaseous atom occurs at a frequency of 2.49 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹. What is the first ionisation energy of the element in kJ mol⁻¹.
items.answer: 994 kJ mol⁻¹

items.stem: The first ionisation energies of potassium and lithium are 419 and 520 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the wavelength of the convergence limit of the ground-state series for each element. items.answer: (a) potassium 286 nm, lithium 230 nm; (b) ultraviolet, ultraviolet

items.stem: Briefly explain why the convergence limit of a series ending at n = 1 gives the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom.
items.answer: At the convergence limit the electron falls from n = ∞ (where it is no longer bound) to the ground state n = 1; the photon energy equals the energy needed to remove an electron from n = 1 to infinity, i.e. the ionisation energy (per atom).

items.stem: "The ionisation energy of hydrogen can be found from the convergence limit of the visible (Balmer) series." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Balmer series ends at n = 2, so its convergence limit gives the energy to remove an electron from n = 2, not from the ground state; the Lyman (n = 1) series must be used.
items.markingKey: The Balmer series ends at n = 2, so its convergence limit gives the energy to remove an electron from n = 2, not from the ground state; the Lyman (n = 1) series must be used. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The convergence limit of the ground-state series of an atom is at 241.3 nm. What is its first ionisation energy?
items.answer: 496 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: B. IE = hcNA/λ = 496 kJ mol⁻¹ (λ in m, divide J by 1000).

items.stem: "Using a convergence limit is a more reliable way to determine ionisation energy than electrical (electron-impact) methods." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: For hydrogen the spectroscopic method is extremely precise; for complex atoms, it is limited and complementary methods are used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: spectral frequencies can be measured very precisely; no need to ionise samples in a field. Arguments against: the limit must often be extrapolated, introducing uncertainty; only practical for simple atoms with clear series; multi-electron atoms give complex spectra. Supported judgement: For hydrogen the spectroscopic method is extremely precise; for complex atoms, it is limited and complementary methods are used. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "atomic orbital"?
options: An arrangement in which one or more electrons occupy higher energy levels than in the ground state
The minimum energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions
Electrons fill orbitals of equal energy singly, with parallel spins, before pairing
A region of space around the nucleus in which there is a high probability of finding an electron; each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons
items.answer: A region of space around the nucleus in which there is a high probability of finding an electron; each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons
items.markingKey: D. "atomic orbital" is a region of space around the nucleus in which there is a high probability of finding an electron; each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons.

items.stem: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is 738 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of aluminium is 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference.

items.stem: Distinguish between an s orbital and a p orbital.
items.answer: An s orbital is spherical and each s sublevel has one orbital; a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped and each p sublevel has three orbitals (px, py, pz) at right angles.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a line spectrum and a continuous spectrum.
items.answer: A continuous spectrum contains all wavelengths in a range; a line spectrum contains only specific wavelengths corresponding to transitions between discrete energy levels.

items.stem: Distinguish between second ionisation energy and first ionisation energy.
items.answer: First IE removes one electron from a gaseous atom (X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻); second IE removes an electron from the gaseous 1+ ion (X⁺(g) → X²⁺(g) + e⁻) and is always larger.

items.stem: Explain how the first ionisation energy of hydrogen can be determined from its emission spectrum. Include the series used, how the convergence limit is found and the calculation from the convergence frequency of 3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
items.answer: Use the Lyman (UV) series, which ends at n = 1 (ground state). Lines converge; plot Δf against f and extrapolate to Δf = 0 to find the limit (3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz). E = hf = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom; × NA = 1.31 × 10⁶ J mol⁻¹ = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Explain why the convergence limit can be difficult to read directly from an emission spectrum, and how it is found in practice.
items.answer: The lines become so close that they merge and cannot be resolved; the limit is found by plotting the difference in frequency between successive lines against frequency and extrapolating to zero difference.

items.answer: n = 3 can hold 2n² = 18 electrons (3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰); 8 is the number in 3s and 3p only.

items.stem: Briefly explain why lines in the hydrogen emission spectrum converge at higher frequencies.
items.answer: The energy levels get closer together as n increases, so the energy differences for transitions from high n to the same lower level become more similar.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the first ionisation energy generally increases across period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main energy level, so shielding stays roughly constant; the effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so outer electrons are held more strongly.

items.stem: "Exceptions such as chromium and copper show that the Aufbau principle is not useful." To what extent is this view justified?
